rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2<U+2013>2.7, Tables 3<U+2013>4, Figs 2<U+2013>7 <U+2014> a 2-year randomised block field experiment (2018<U+2013>2019) in a wolfberry orchard on the Tibetan Plateau with three treatments and the authors' own soil moisture, isotope, root, yield and WUE measurements.
rows.notes: All three treatments (CK, MF, MR) receive surface drip irrigation; the only contrast is full-film (black gardening cloth) mulch and ridge-furrow versus flat planting without mulch, all under drip. There is no comparison of drip (or DIPM) against a traditional irrigation method, so the result is evidence about mulch/ridge-furrow under drip, not about drip or DIPM versus traditional irrigation. What the study shows: soil water content across 0<U+2013>100 cm was 30.2% (MF) and 37.1% (MR) higher than CK (Section 3.2, Fig. 3); soil temperature differences are only referred to via supplementary Table S3; nutrient availability is reported only as site baseline properties (Table 1), not as a treatment effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.3, 3.4 and Fig. 2 <U+2014> the authors sampled fine roots (0<U+2013>100/120 cm) in October 2018 and 2019 with a hand auger and computed fine root length density per treatment.
rows.notes: The study reports that FRLD in the shallow layer was significantly lower under CK than under MF and MR and that FRLD order was MR > MF > CK (Section 3.4, Fig. 2), but all treatments are drip-irrigated; the contrast is mulch/ridge-furrow versus no mulch under drip, not DIPM versus traditional irrigation. Hence it is evidence about mulch, not about drip as the technology named. The study does not report crop emergence or growth-period length. Water-source uptake shifts toward shallow layers under MF/MR are inferred from isotope mixing models (Fig. 5), and nutrient uptake is only speculated in Discussion 4.3.
